Chapter 20

Functions that cross the network

query and command: server code you import into a component and call like any other function.

By the end of this chapter

A .remote.ts file whose exports run on the server, are typed end to end, and validate every argument.

Here is the whole idea, in one file and one component.

That is it. No endpoint to name, no fetch to write, no load function at all, no response type to keep in sync. The component imports a function and awaits it. SvelteKit puts an HTTP request in the middle and neither side has to know.

The slug comes from the page's own props. Every page receives params, the route's parameters, and PageProps from the generated ./$types types them from the folder name: this page lives in book/[slug], so params.slug is a string, and a typo is a compile error. The page hands it to the query as an argument, because a remote function cannot read the URL for itself — more on that in a moment.

Why params, and not a load function

This page used to have a +page.ts whose whole body was return { slug: params.slug }, and the page typed its props by hand as { data: { slug: string } }. Both were wrong in a way that compiled. The load was a moving part that renamed a value the router already hands every page — SvelteKit 2.24 added the params prop for exactly this, "particularly useful alongside remote functions" in the docs' words — and the hand-written type was not connected to the load at all: rename the key it returned, and the page still type-checked and rendered undefined. PageProps and LayoutProps are generated from the files that actually feed the component, so they cannot drift. Every page and layout in the app now takes its props that way.

The server code never reaches the browser. The import is replaced at build time with a small stub that makes the request. Your database credentials, your Drizzle queries and your if (!found) are all server-side, and the bundle is checked to make sure of it.

The security model is inverted

This is the part to take seriously, because it is the opposite of a load function.

  • A load function runs for one URL. It can trust params, because the router produced them.
  • A remote function is a public HTTP endpoint. Anybody can call it with anything, from anywhere, in any order.

So every argument gets a schema, and — this is the important bit — the server must never look at event.params or event.url to decide what to return.

SvelteKit enforces this: reading event.params or event.url inside a query throws. It is not a lint rule you can ignore. Everything the server needs must arrive as a validated argument, because the URL a remote call happens to be made from is not evidence of anything.

Schemas, with valibot

SvelteKit accepts any Standard Schema library, which is a small shared interface that valibot, Zod, ArkType and others implement. We use valibot: it is a fraction of the size, and because every rule is a separate function, a bundler drops the ones you do not use.

A schema is not paperwork. It is the only thing standing between serviceId and somebody sending an object where a string was expected, to see what happens.

Commands: the ones that change things

query reads, command writes. The split is not cosmetic: queries are cached and de-duplicated by their arguments, and commands are not, because "add this shift" twice is two shifts.

One thing a command cannot do is send the browser somewhere else. The docs allow redirect(...) in query, form and prerender handlers, "It is not possible inside command functions", and the browser throws if one tries. Anything that ends in a redirect — signing out, for one — is a form. Chapter 21 shows the sign-out button that learned this the hard way.

Single-flight mutations

That getHours(...).refresh() line is worth stopping on. It runs on the server, inside the command, and it means the response to "add this shift" carries the new list of hours with it.

The usual pattern is: post the change, wait, then fetch the new state, wait again. Two round trips, and a visible flicker in between where the screen shows the old data. Refreshing inside the handler collapses that into one.

This app never actually writes those lines — its commands call .refresh() on the server, the way addHours does above, so every caller gets the fresh data without asking. .updates() is for the day only the calling component knows which queries are on screen — a filtered list, say — and it is a two-sided contract: the server must refresh, set or deliberately ignore() every instance the client asked for (refreshAll() and ignoreAll() are the bulk spellings), or that query errors on the client. The limit argument is not optional because the list comes from the browser, and each entry costs the server a validation and a re-fetch; an unbounded one would be a denial-of-service lever.

One trap on the way back

When a command calls error(400, 'A shift has to end after it starts.'), the browser sees SvelteKit's HttpError. And HttpError does not extend Error.

The message you wrote is discarded and the generic fallback appears instead. Nothing looks broken — a plausible sentence is still on screen — which is exactly why this survives review. We only found it because an end-to-end test asserted on the real wording.

isHttpError is SvelteKit's own test, exported from @sveltejs/kit right beside error. What the browser receives is an instance of the very HttpError class that error() throws on the server (strictly, of a subclass SvelteKit uses for errors that have already been through handleError), so the test is an instanceof, and once it passes TypeScript knows that thrown.body is your App.Error.

The status < 500 is there because instanceof is not quite the guarantee it looks like. One more thing arrives as an HttpError: a response that never reached SvelteKit at all, such as a proxy's 502 page. The browser builds it from the same class, with the HTTP status text as its message, so isHttpError cannot tell it apart, and without the status check a customer's alert said "Bad Gateway". Every sentence this app writes on purpose is a 4xx — the shift that ends before it starts is a 400 — and the only 5xx sentence it ever sends is handleError's generic apology, which the caller's own fallback says better. So a 5xx gets the fallback, whoever sent it. The trim() is the same idea for the 4xx a proxy might send: over HTTP/2 there is no status text at all, and an alert with nothing in it is worse than the fallback.

Why not check the shape by hand

An earlier version of this helper did: an object with a numeric status and a body, spelled out longhand, because SvelteKit does not export the HttpError class to test against. It does export the test, though, and the hand-made one is worse in a way that matters. It accepts any object of the right shape, so a unit test built on a literal { status, body } passes against something the browser never produces, and the helper would put a sentence nobody vetted on a customer's screen. instanceof accepts only what SvelteKit made.

Notice what else is not there: a second branch for thrown instanceof Error. That branch looks like a kindness, and the earlier version had it too. The other things a remote call rejects with are a dropped connection, which arrives as the browser's own TypeError: Failed to fetch, and a bug in our code, which arrives as whatever the bug said. Neither has been through handleError, so neither is a sentence anybody vetted for a customer's screen. The fallback is for exactly those, so the helper reads a 4xx's body.message and nothing else.

Both halves are pinned by end-to-end tests in a real browser. One opens the same booking in two windows and cancels it in both, so the second cancellation is refused with "That booking is already cancelled."; run against the instanceof Error catch at the top of this section, its alert shows the fallback instead. The other switches the network off before pressing Cancel; run against the earlier helper with the extra branch, its alert reads "Failed to fetch". We ran each test against the bug it names and watched it fail, which is the only way to know a test can.

setOffline is Playwright cutting the browser's network, not a mock, so the command's real fetch really fails, the way it does for a customer on a train. The two assertions together make the test fail for the right reason: the fallback has to be on screen, and the browser's wording has to be absent. Either one alone could pass with the bug still in place.

Write it once, in src/lib/errors.ts, and use it in every catch around a remote call. Six places in this app catch a remote rejection; all six had the same bug, because all six were written from the same reasonable instinct.

A catch is not a boundary

This helper is for the value a catch receives. A <svelte:boundary>'s failed snippet and +error.svelte are handed something else: an App.Error, { status, message }, with no body at all. Pass one of those to messageFrom and the fallback wins every time. Chapter 23 shows the boundary side, and how this project got it wrong.

Checkpoint

The booking page renders from a query, and a command that calls error(400, …) shows your message in the browser, not a generic one. Open the same booking in two windows, cancel it in one, then press Cancel in the other: the alert says "That booking is already cancelled.", the server's sentence. Switch the network off in your browser's developer tools and try again, and you get the fallback, not "Failed to fetch". pnpm test:e2e checks both on every run.
